point: advice (n): helpful words about what to do
wrong: She gave me an advice about my exam.
right: She gave me some advice about my exam.
why: Advice is uncountable, so it has no plural and no a or an.
aha: Say a piece of advice, never an advice.
ex: Can I ask you for some advice?
My teacher's advice was very useful.

quiz.q: She gave me some ___ about my exam.
quiz.explain: Advice is uncountable, so it has no plural and no a or an.

point: accommodation (n): a place to stay or live
wrong: I need to find an accommodation near the university.
right: I need to find accommodation near the university.
why: In British English, accommodation is uncountable, so it does not take a or an.
aha: Treat it like furniture: no a, no s.
ex: The price includes accommodation and meals.
We are looking for cheap accommodation.

quiz.q: I need to find ___ near the university.
quiz.explain: In British English, accommodation is uncountable, so it does not take a or an.

point: angry (adj): feeling that you want to shout at someone
wrong: She is angry on her brother.
right: She is angry with her brother.
why: Use angry with for a person and angry about for a thing.
aha: With a person, about a problem.
ex: I was angry about the delay.
Please don't be angry with me.

quiz.explain: Use angry with for a person and angry about for a thing.

point: arrive (v): to reach a place
wrong: We arrived to Hanoi at noon.
right: We arrived in Hanoi at noon.
why: Use arrive in for cities and countries, and arrive at for small places.
aha: Arrive in a city, arrive at a station.
ex: They arrived at the airport early.
When did you arrive in London?

quiz.explain: Use arrive in for cities and countries, and arrive at for small places.

point: agree (v): to have the same opinion
wrong: I am agree with you.
right: I agree with you.
why: Agree is a verb, so do not put am, is or are before it.
aha: Agree is an action, not a feeling word.
ex: I agree with your idea.
Do you agree with me?

quiz.explain: Agree is a verb, so do not put am, is or are before it.

point: attend (v): to go to an event or class
hook: Natives don't say 'attend to the meeting'
wrong: I attended to the meeting yesterday.
right: I attended the meeting yesterday.
why: When attend means go to, it has no preposition after it.
aha: Attend a class, no to needed.
ex: She attends English classes every week.
Over two hundred people attended the concert.

quiz.explain: When attend means go to, it has no preposition after it.

point: answer (v): to reply to a question
hook: Natives don't say 'answer to my question'
wrong: She answered to my question.
right: She answered my question.
why: Answer takes a direct object, so do not add to.
aha: Answer the question, but reply to the question.
ex: Can you answer this question?
He answered the phone quickly.

quiz.explain: Answer takes a direct object, so do not add to.

point: argue (v): to speak angrily with someone
wrong: I argued to my brother about money.
right: I argued with my brother about money.
why: Use argue with a person and argue about a topic.
ex: They argue about politics all the time.
Don't argue with the referee.

quiz.q: I argued ___ my brother about money.
quiz.explain: Use argue with a person and argue about a topic.

point: borrow (v): to take something for a short time
wrong: Can you borrow me your pen?
right: Can you lend me your pen?
why: Borrow means take for a short time. Lend means give for a short time.
aha: I borrow from you; you lend to me.
ex: Can I borrow your umbrella?
I often borrow books from the library.

quiz.explain: Borrow means take for a short time. Lend means give for a short time.

point: belong (v): to be owned by someone
wrong: This book is belonged to me.
right: This book belongs to me.
why: Belong is never used in the passive. Say belongs to.
aha: Belong has no be before it.
ex: Who does this coat belong to?
I feel that I belong here.

quiz.explain: Belong is never used in the passive. Say belongs to.

point: cheap (adj): not costing much money
hook: Natives don't say 'the price is cheap'
wrong: The price of the room is very cheap.
right: The price of the room is very low.
why: A thing is cheap, but a price is low.
ex: This shirt is cheap.
This cheap hotel is clean.

quiz.q: The price of the room is very ___.
quiz.explain: A thing is cheap, but a price is low.

point: clothes (n): things you wear
wrong: Your clothes is dirty.
right: Your clothes are dirty.
why: Clothes is always plural, so use are, not is.
ex: I need some new clothes.
Her clothes are always neat.

quiz.explain: Clothes is always plural, so use are, not is.

point: consist (v): to be made of parts
wrong: The team is consisted of five people.
right: The team consists of five people.
why: Consist of is never passive. Say consists of.
aha: Consists of, never is consisted of.
ex: The course consists of ten lessons.
Breakfast consisted of rice and eggs.

quiz.explain: Consist of is never passive. Say consists of.

point: afford (v): to have enough money for something
wrong: I can't afford buying a new phone.
right: I can't afford to buy a new phone.
why: After afford, use to and the base verb, not -ing.
aha: Afford is followed by to plus verb.
ex: We can't afford to go on holiday.
Can you afford a new car?

quiz.q: I can't afford ___ a new phone.
quiz.explain: After afford, use to and the base verb, not -ing.

point: avoid (v): to stay away from something
wrong: He avoided to talk to me.
right: He avoided talking to me.
why: After avoid, use the -ing form, not to plus verb.
ex: I avoid eating late at night.
She avoided the traffic.

quiz.explain: After avoid, use the -ing form, not to plus verb.

point: advise (v): to tell someone what they should do
wrong: He advised me do more exercise.
right: He advised me to do more exercise.
why: After advise someone, use to and the base verb.
ex: The doctor advised me to rest.
I advise you to book early.

quiz.explain: After advise someone, use to and the base verb.

point: baggage (n): bags and cases you take on a trip
wrong: I have too many baggages.
right: I have too much baggage.
why: Baggage is uncountable, so use much and no s.
ex: Please collect your baggage here.
We lost some baggage at the airport.

quiz.explain: Baggage is uncountable, so use much and no s.

point: bread (n): a food made from flour
wrong: I bought two breads this morning.
right: I bought two loaves of bread this morning.
why: Bread is uncountable. Count it with loaves or slices.
aha: Count bread by loaves or slices.
ex: I eat bread for breakfast.
Please cut me a slice of bread.

quiz.explain: Bread is uncountable. Count it with loaves or slices.

point: blame (v): to say someone did something wrong
wrong: She blamed me about the mistake.
right: She blamed me for the mistake.
why: Use blame someone for something.
ex: Don't blame yourself for it.
They blamed the weather for the delay.

quiz.explain: Use blame someone for something.

point: compare (v): to look at how things are different
hook: Natives don't say 'Compare with my brother'
wrong: Compare with my brother, I am short.
right: Compared with my brother, I am short.
why: Use the -ed form, compared with, because I am being compared.
aha: Start the sentence with compared with.
ex: Compared with last year, prices are higher.
Don't compare yourself with others.

quiz.q: ___ with my brother, I am short.
quiz.explain: Use the -ed form, compared with, because I am being compared.

point: apply (v): to ask for a job or place
wrong: I applied a job at the bank.
right: I applied for a job at the bank.
why: Use apply for a job. Apply needs for before the job.
aha: Apply for a job, apply to a company.
ex: She applied to three universities.
You can apply for the course online.

quiz.q: I applied ___ a job at the bank.
quiz.explain: Use apply for a job. Apply needs for before the job.

point: attention (n): looking and listening carefully
wrong: Pay attention on the teacher.
right: Pay attention to the teacher.
why: Use pay attention to someone or something.
ex: Please pay attention to the signs.
The baby needs a lot of attention.

quiz.explain: Use pay attention to someone or something.

point: aware (adj): knowing that something exists
wrong: I wasn't aware about the problem.
right: I wasn't aware of the problem.
why: Aware is followed by of, not about.
ex: Are you aware of the rules?
She became aware that someone was following her.

quiz.explain: Aware is followed by of, not about.

point: absent (adj): not at a place when you should be
wrong: He was absent in class yesterday.
right: He was absent from class yesterday.
why: Use absent from a place or an event.
ex: She is often absent from work.
Three students were absent today.

quiz.explain: Use absent from a place or an event.

point: close (adj): near in distance
wrong: My house is close with the school.
right: My house is close to the school.
why: Use close to for a place that is near.
ex: Is the hotel close to the beach?
We are close to finishing.

quiz.q: My house is close ___ the school.
quiz.explain: Use close to for a place that is near.

point: crime (n): an illegal act
wrong: He did a crime last year.
right: He committed a crime last year.
why: Use commit with crime. We do not say do a crime.
aha: Commit a crime, make a mistake.
ex: Crime has gone down in this city.
The police are looking into the crime.

quiz.explain: Use commit with crime. We do not say do a crime.

point: accident (n): a bad event that was not planned
wrong: I made an accident on my way home.
right: I had an accident on my way home.
why: Use have an accident. We do not make an accident.
ex: There was an accident on the road.
She broke the glass by accident.

quiz.q: I ___ an accident on my way home.
quiz.explain: Use have an accident. We do not make an accident.

point: abroad (adv): in or to another country
wrong: She wants to go to abroad next year.
right: She wants to go abroad next year.
why: Abroad is an adverb, so do not use to before it.
aha: Abroad already means to another country.
ex: He works abroad.
Have you ever lived abroad?

quiz.q: She wants to go ___ next year.
quiz.explain: Abroad is an adverb, so do not use to before it.

point: amount (n): how much of something
wrong: A large amount of students joined the club.
right: A large number of students joined the club.
why: Use amount with uncountable nouns and number with countable nouns.
aha: Number of students, amount of money.
ex: A large amount of money is missing.
The amount of rain this year is small.

quiz.q: A large ___ of students joined the club.
quiz.explain: Use amount with uncountable nouns and number with countable nouns.

point: bus (n): a big vehicle that carries people
wrong: I go to school by the bus.
right: I go to school by bus.
why: With by and a kind of transport, do not use the.
aha: By bus, by train, by car.
ex: I take the bus to work every day.
Is there a bus to the airport?

quiz.explain: With by and a kind of transport, do not use the.

point: almost (adv): nearly
wrong: Almost people like music.
right: Most people like music.
why: Almost is an adverb. Before a noun, use most.
aha: Most plus noun, almost plus all.
ex: It's almost midnight.
Almost everyone came to the party.

quiz.explain: Almost is an adverb. Before a noun, use most.

point: billion (n): one thousand million
wrong: The country has two billions people.
right: The country has two billion people.
why: After a number, billion stays singular.
ex: The world has about eight billion people.
The film earned a billion dollars.

quiz.explain: After a number, billion stays singular.

point: capable (adj): able to do something
wrong: She is capable to solve the problem.
right: She is capable of solving the problem.
why: Capable is followed by of plus an -ing verb.
ex: He is capable of running a marathon.
You are capable of better work.

quiz.explain: Capable is followed by of plus an -ing verb.

point: accustomed (adj): used to something
wrong: I am not accustomed to get up early.
right: I am not accustomed to getting up early.
why: In accustomed to, to is a preposition, so use an -ing verb.
ex: She is accustomed to hot weather.
We soon got accustomed to the noise.

quiz.q: I am not accustomed to ___ up early.
quiz.explain: In accustomed to, to is a preposition, so use an -ing verb.

point: addicted (adj): unable to stop doing something
wrong: He is addicted with video games.
right: He is addicted to video games.
why: Use addicted to something.
ex: She is addicted to coffee.
Many people get addicted to their phones.

quiz.explain: Use addicted to something.

point: bad (adj): not good
wrong: I am bad in maths.
right: I am bad at maths.
why: Use bad at for skills and school subjects.
ex: He is bad at cooking.
She is not bad at tennis.

quiz.explain: Use bad at for skills and school subjects.

point: break (n): a short rest
wrong: Let's do a break for ten minutes.
right: Let's take a break for ten minutes.
why: Use take a break or have a break.
aha: Take a break, not do a break.
ex: I need a break from work.
We had a short break at eleven.

quiz.q: Let's ___ a break for ten minutes.
quiz.explain: Use take a break or have a break.

point: bath (n): washing yourself in a tub
wrong: I made a bath after work.
right: I took a bath after work.
why: Use take a bath or have a bath in English.
aha: Take a bath, have a bath.
ex: The baby has a bath every night.
She ran a hot bath.

quiz.explain: Use take a bath or have a bath in English.

point: approach (v): to come near
wrong: The taxi approached to the hotel.
right: The taxi approached the hotel.
why: Approach takes a direct object, so do not add to.
ex: A man approached me in the street.
Winter is approaching.

quiz.explain: Approach takes a direct object, so do not add to.

point: contact (v): to call or write to someone
wrong: Please contact with me by email.
right: Please contact me by email.
why: Contact takes a direct object, with no with.
ex: I'll contact you tomorrow.
You can contact the school by phone.

quiz.explain: Contact takes a direct object, with no with.

point: crowded (adj): full of people
wrong: The market was very crowd.
right: The market was very crowded.
why: After was, use the adjective crowded, not the noun crowd.
aha: Crowd is a noun, crowded is an adjective.
ex: The train was crowded.
I don't like crowded places.

quiz.explain: After was, use the adjective crowded, not the noun crowd.

point: comfortable (adj): feeling relaxed and at ease
wrong: I felt very comfortably in the new house.
right: I felt very comfortable in the new house.
why: After feel, use an adjective, not an adverb.
ex: This chair is very comfortable.
Make yourself comfortable.

quiz.q: I felt very ___ in the new house.
quiz.explain: After feel, use an adjective, not an adverb.

point: child (n): a young person
wrong: Three childs were playing outside.
right: Three children were playing outside.
why: The plural of child is children.
ex: She has two children.
Every child needs sleep.

quiz.explain: The plural of child is children.

point: advantage (n): a good thing that helps you
wrong: She took advantage from the sale.
right: She took advantage of the sale.
why: Use take advantage of something.
ex: Let's take advantage of the good weather.
One advantage of the city is the transport.

quiz.explain: Use take advantage of something.

point: charge (n): control of someone or something
wrong: She is in charge for the project.
right: She is in charge of the project.
why: Use in charge of, not in charge for.
ex: Who is in charge here?
There is no charge for children.

quiz.q: She is in charge ___ the project.
quiz.explain: Use in charge of, not in charge for.

point: aim (n): the purpose of something
wrong: The aim of this course is improve your speaking.
right: The aim of this course is to improve your speaking.
why: After the aim is, use to and the base verb.
aha: The aim is to do something.
ex: My aim is to pass the test.
The aim of the game is simple.

quiz.q: The aim of this course is ___ your speaking.
quiz.explain: After the aim is, use to and the base verb.

point: cash (n): money in coins and notes
wrong: I paid by cash at the shop.
right: I paid in cash at the shop.
why: Use in cash for notes and coins, and by card for cards.
ex: Do you have any cash?
I need to get some cash from the bank.

quiz.q: I paid ___ cash at the shop.
quiz.explain: Use in cash for notes and coins, and by card for cards.

point: amazed (adj): very surprised
wrong: I was very amazing at the view.
right: I was very amazed at the view.
why: Use -ed for how a person feels. Use -ing for the thing.
aha: I am amazed; the view is amazing.
ex: She was amazed by the news.
The view is amazing.
memory: I am amazed, it is amazing

quiz.q: I was very ___ at the view.
quiz.explain: Use -ed for how a person feels. Use -ing for the thing.

point: confusing (adj): hard to understand
wrong: The map is very confused.
right: The map is very confusing.
why: Use -ing for the thing that confuses you, and -ed for the person.
ex: The rules are confusing.
I felt confused after the lesson.

quiz.explain: Use -ing for the thing that confuses you, and -ed for the person.

point: appointment (n): a time you arrange to see someone
wrong: I want to do an appointment with the dentist.
right: I want to make an appointment with the dentist.
why: Use make an appointment. We do not say do an appointment.
aha: Make an appointment, make a plan.
ex: I have an appointment at ten.
She made an appointment with her teacher.

quiz.q: I want to ___ an appointment with the dentist.
quiz.explain: Use make an appointment. We do not say do an appointment.

point: depend (v): to be decided by something
wrong: It depend of the weather.
right: It depends on the weather.
why: Use depend with on. Add -s after he, she or it.
aha: Vietnamese 'tuy thuoc vao': think depend ON.
ex: It depends on the price.
Success depends on hard work.

quiz.explain: Depend takes on, and he/she/it needs -s.

point: describe (v): to say what someone or something is like
wrong: Can you describe about your village?
right: Can you describe your village?
why: Describe is followed directly by the thing. No about.
aha: Describe it: no little word after.
ex: Please describe the man you saw.
She described her new flat to us.

quiz.explain: Describe needs no preposition before its object.

point: discuss (v): to talk about something with others
wrong: We discussed about the plan.
right: We discussed the plan.
why: Discuss already means talk about. Do not add about.
aha: Discuss = talk about. Never add about.
ex: We need to discuss this problem.
They discussed the trip for an hour.

quiz.explain: Discuss already includes the meaning of about.

point: divorce (v): to legally end a marriage
wrong: She divorced with her husband last year.
right: She divorced her husband last year.
why: Divorce takes a direct object. We do not use with here.
ex: He divorced his wife in 2020.
They got divorced two years ago.

quiz.explain: Divorce is followed directly by the person.

point: enjoy (v): to like doing something
wrong: I enjoy to swim on Sundays.
right: I enjoy swimming on Sundays.
why: After enjoy, use the -ing form of the verb.
ex: I enjoy cooking for my family.
Did you enjoy the film?

quiz.explain: Enjoy is followed by a verb with -ing.

point: enough (adv): as much as needed
wrong: This room is enough big for us.
right: This room is big enough for us.
why: Enough comes after an adjective, but before a noun.
ex: He is not tall enough to reach it.
The soup is hot enough now.

quiz.explain: Enough goes after an adjective.

point: explain (v): to make something clear
wrong: Can you explain me this rule?
right: Can you explain this rule to me?
why: After explain, say the thing first. Then use to for the person.
ex: The teacher explained the rule to us.
Please explain it to my brother.

quiz.explain: With explain, the person needs to.

point: experience (n): knowledge from doing something
wrong: I have many experience in cooking.
right: I have a lot of experience in cooking.
why: In this meaning, experience is uncountable. Use a lot of, not many.
aha: Skill-experience is uncountable: a lot of.
ex: She has a lot of experience with children.
You need some experience for this job.
memory: Experience: a lot of, not many

quiz.explain: Experience for skill is uncountable, so no many.

point: fail (v): not to pass a test
hook: Natives don't say 'fail in the exam'
wrong: I failed in the exam last week.
right: I failed the exam last week.
why: Fail is followed directly by the test. No in.
aha: Fail a test, pass a test.
ex: Many students fail this test.
He failed his driving test twice.

quiz.explain: Fail takes the exam as its direct object.

point: finish (v): to complete something
wrong: I finished to write the report.
right: I finished writing the report.
why: After finish, use the -ing form of the verb.
ex: Have you finished eating?
She finished cleaning at noon.

quiz.explain: Finish is followed by a verb with -ing.

point: forget (v): to leave something behind by mistake (leave)
hook: Natives don't say 'forgot my umbrella at home'
wrong: I forgot my umbrella at home.
right: I left my umbrella at home.
why: Say where it is with leave. Forget is for not remembering.
ex: I left my phone on the bus.
Don't forget to call your mother.

quiz.q: I ___ my keys at the office.
quiz.explain: Use leave for an object left in a place.

point: furniture (n): tables, chairs and beds
wrong: We bought some new furnitures.
right: We bought some new furniture.
why: Furniture is uncountable. It has no plural -s.
ex: The furniture in this room is old.
I need a piece of furniture for my desk.

quiz.explain: Furniture is an uncountable noun.

point: graduate (v): to finish university or school
wrong: She graduated university in 2019.
right: She graduated from university in 2019.
why: Use from after graduate before a school or university.
ex: He graduated from high school last year.
When did you graduate from college?

quiz.explain: Graduate needs from before the school name.

point: happen (v): to take place
wrong: The accident was happened yesterday.
right: The accident happened yesterday.
why: Happen is never passive. Use it in the simple past: happened.
ex: What happened to your arm?
It happened on Monday.

quiz.explain: Happen is not used in the passive.

point: homework (n): school work done at home
wrong: I must make my homework tonight.
right: I must do my homework tonight.
why: We do homework. We do not make it.
aha: Homework: do it, never make it.
ex: Have you done your homework?
She does her homework after dinner.

quiz.explain: The usual verb with homework is do.

point: housework (n): cleaning and cooking at home
wrong: I make housework every weekend.
right: I do housework every weekend.
why: We do housework. Housework is uncountable too.
ex: He never does any housework.
We share the housework at home.

quiz.explain: The usual verb with housework is do.

point: however (adv): but; in contrast
hook: Natives don't say 'It was cold, however we'
wrong: It was cold, however we went out.
right: It was cold. However, we went out.
why: However cannot join two sentences with a comma. Start a new sentence.
ex: It was late. However, he kept working.
I like tea; however, I prefer coffee.

quiz.q: It was cold. ___, we went out.
quiz.explain: Use a full stop or semicolon before however.

point: despite (prep): although something is true
wrong: Despite of the rain, we played.
right: Despite the rain, we played.
why: Despite is followed directly by a noun. Do not add of.
aha: Despite: no of. In spite OF.
ex: Despite the noise, he slept well.
We went out despite the cold.

quiz.explain: Despite never takes of; in spite of does.

point: during (prep): at some point in a period of time
wrong: I studied during three hours.
right: I studied for three hours.
why: For tells how long. During tells when something happens.
ex: I slept for eight hours.
He called during dinner.

quiz.explain: Use for with a length of time.

point: equipment (n): tools and things for a job
wrong: The gym has many equipments.
right: The gym has a lot of equipment.
why: Equipment is uncountable. It has no plural -s.
ex: We need new equipment for the lab.
This equipment is very expensive.

quiz.q: The gym has a lot of ___.
quiz.explain: Equipment is an uncountable noun.

point: evidence (n): facts that show something is true
wrong: The police found many evidences.
right: The police found a lot of evidence.
why: Evidence is uncountable. It has no plural -s.
ex: There is no evidence of a crime.
We need more evidence.

quiz.q: The police found a lot of ___.
quiz.explain: Evidence is an uncountable noun.

point: hardly (adv): almost not
wrong: She works hardly every day.
right: She works hard every day.
why: Hardly means almost not. For doing something with effort, use hard.
aha: Hardly is not hard's adverb twin.
ex: I can hardly hear you.
He hardly ever eats meat.

quiz.explain: Hardly means almost not; the adverb of effort is hard.

point: heavy (adj): large in amount or force
wrong: There was strong rain last night.
right: There was heavy rain last night.
why: We say heavy rain, not strong rain. It is a fixed pair.
aha: Rain is heavy, tea is strong.
ex: Heavy traffic made us late.
We had heavy snow in January.

quiz.explain: The natural collocation is heavy rain.

point: habit (n): something you do often
wrong: I have a habit to wake up early.
right: I have a habit of waking up early.
why: After habit of, use the -ing form of the verb.
ex: She has a habit of biting her nails.
Smoking is a bad habit.

quiz.q: I have a habit ___ up early.
quiz.explain: Habit is followed by of and the -ing form.

point: grow (v): to become an adult (grow up)
wrong: I was grown up in Hue.
right: I grew up in Hue.
why: Grow up is never passive. Use the simple past: grew up.
aha: Grow up: active, never was grown.
ex: She grew up in a small town.
Children grow up fast.

quiz.explain: Grow up is not used in the passive.

point: die (v): to stop living
wrong: My grandfather is died.
right: My grandfather died.
why: Die is a verb, not an adjective. Use died or is dead.
ex: He died in 2010.
The plant died because of the cold.
memory: Died or dead, never is died

quiz.explain: Die is not used with is; use died or is dead.

point: disagree (v): to have a different opinion
wrong: I disagree to you about this.
right: I disagree with you about this.
why: Use with after disagree when you name the person.
ex: I disagree with my brother.
She disagreed with the plan.

quiz.explain: Disagree is followed by with.

point: enter (v): to go into a place
wrong: Please enter to the room.
right: Please enter the room.
why: Enter is followed directly by the place. No to.
ex: He entered the building quietly.
Do not enter this room.

quiz.explain: Enter takes a direct object, so no to.

point: familiar (adj): knowing something well
wrong: I am familiar to this city.
right: I am familiar with this city.
why: Say you are familiar with something. Familiar to means known by someone.
ex: Are you familiar with this app?
His face looks familiar to me.

quiz.explain: Use familiar with for something you know well.

point: full (adj): with no more space
wrong: The bus is full with people.
right: The bus is full of people.
why: Use full of, not full with.
ex: The box is full of old books.
My bag is full of snacks.

quiz.explain: The correct pair is full of.

point: grateful (adj): thankful
hook: Natives don't say 'grateful to your help'
wrong: I am grateful to your help.
right: I am grateful for your help.
why: Use grateful for a thing. Use grateful to a person.
ex: We are grateful for your support.
She was grateful to her teacher.

quiz.explain: Grateful for goes before the thing someone did.

point: hire (v): to pay to use something for a short time
wrong: We want to hire a flat for a year.
right: We want to rent a flat for a year.
why: In British English, hire is for short use. Use rent for homes.
aha: Hire a car, rent a flat.
ex: We hired a car for the weekend.
They hired a boat for two hours.

quiz.q: We want to ___ a flat for a year.
quiz.explain: For a flat or house, we say rent.

point: economical (adj): not costing much to use
wrong: I bought an economic car.
right: I bought an economical car.
why: Economical means saving money. Economic is about the economy.
aha: Economical saves money; economic is about money systems.
ex: This heater is very economical.
A small car is more economical.

quiz.explain: Economical means cheap to use.

point: guilty (adj): having done something wrong
wrong: He felt guilty for a crime.
right: He was guilty of a crime.
why: Use guilty of with a crime. Use guilty about for a feeling.
ex: The jury found him guilty of theft.
I feel guilty about the mess.

quiz.explain: Guilty is followed by of for a crime.

point: difference (n): how two things are not the same
wrong: What is the difference of tea and coffee?
right: What is the difference between tea and coffee?
why: Use between with difference when you compare two things.
ex: There is a big difference between them.
I see no difference between the two.

quiz.q: What is the difference ___ tea and coffee?
quiz.explain: Difference compares two things with between.

point: different (adj): not the same
wrong: My phone is different with yours.
right: My phone is different from yours.
why: Say different from. Do not say different with.
ex: This book is different from that one.
Life here is different from my town.

quiz.explain: Different is followed by from.

point: effort (n): hard work to do something
wrong: You should do an effort to learn.
right: You should make an effort to learn.
why: We make an effort. We do not do an effort.
aha: Make an effort, make a plan.
ex: I made an effort to smile.
It takes effort to learn a language.

quiz.q: You should ___ an effort to learn.
quiz.explain: The usual verb with effort is make.

point: favour (n): a kind thing you do for someone
hook: Natives don't say 'make me a favour'
wrong: Can you make me a favour?
right: Can you do me a favour?
why: The usual phrase is do someone a favour.
aha: Do a favour, make a mistake.
ex: Could you do me a favour?
He did us a big favour.

quiz.explain: The fixed phrase is do someone a favour.

point: drive (v): to control a car
wrong: He drives a bike to school.
right: He rides a bike to school.
why: We drive cars and trucks. We ride bikes and horses.
ex: She drives a bus in the city.
I ride my bike to work.

quiz.explain: For a bike, the verb is ride.

point: deal (v): to take action about a problem
wrong: We must deal the problem now.
right: We must deal with the problem now.
why: Deal needs with before the problem you solve.
ex: I can deal with this.
How do you deal with stress?

quiz.explain: Deal is followed by with before its object.

point: hand (n): side or point of view (on the other hand)
hook: Natives don't say 'In the other hand'
wrong: In the other hand, it is cheaper.
right: On the other hand, it is cheaper.
why: The fixed phrase is on the one hand, on the other hand.
aha: On the other hand, always on.
ex: On one hand it is cheap, but on the other hand it is slow.
On the other hand, we can wait.

quiz.q: ___ the other hand, it is cheaper.
quiz.explain: The fixed phrase uses on, not in.

point: discount (n): a lower price
wrong: The shop made me a discount.
right: The shop gave me a discount.
why: We give or get a discount. We do not make one.
aha: Give a discount, get a discount.
ex: Students get a discount here.
They gave us a ten percent discount.

quiz.explain: The usual verb with discount is give.

point: dozen (n): a group of twelve
hook: Natives don't say 'two dozens of eggs'
wrong: I bought two dozens of eggs.
right: I bought two dozen eggs.
why: After a number, dozen stays singular and has no of.
aha: Two dozen, no s, no of.
ex: She bought a dozen eggs.
We need two dozen cups.

quiz.explain: After a number, dozen has no -s and no of.

point: essay (n): a short piece of writing
wrong: I need to make an essay tonight.
right: I need to write an essay tonight.
why: We write an essay. We do not make one.
ex: She wrote an essay about her town.
Our teacher marked the essays.

quiz.q: I need to ___ an essay tonight.
quiz.explain: The usual verb with essay is write.

point: exam (n): a formal test
hook: Natives don't say 'pass an exam tomorrow'
wrong: I will pass an exam tomorrow.
right: I will take an exam tomorrow.
why: Take an exam means sit it. Pass means succeed.
ex: I take my last exam on Friday.
She passed the exam easily.

quiz.explain: Pass means you succeed, so use take for sitting it.

point: height (n): how tall something is
wrong: What is the high of that tower?
right: What is the height of that tower?
why: High is an adjective. The noun is height.
aha: High is adjective, height is noun.
ex: The height of the wall is two metres.
He is of average height.

quiz.q: What is the ___ of that tower?
quiz.explain: Height is the noun form of high.

point: fall (v): to begin to feel love (fall in love)
hook: Natives don't say 'fall in love to'
wrong: He fell in love to her.
right: He fell in love with her.
why: Use fall in love with a person.
ex: They fell in love in Paris.
She fell in love with the city.

quiz.explain: The fixed phrase is fall in love with.

point: emphasize (v): to show something is important
wrong: The teacher emphasized on speaking.
right: The teacher emphasized speaking.
why: Emphasize is followed directly by the thing. No on.
ex: We must emphasize safety.
The report emphasizes the cost.

quiz.explain: Emphasize takes a direct object, so no on.

point: dislike (v): not to like
wrong: I dislike to wait in lines.
right: I dislike waiting in lines.
why: After dislike, use the -ing form of the verb.
ex: He dislikes cooking.
I dislike getting up early.

quiz.explain: Dislike is followed by a verb with -ing.

point: delay (v): to do something later
wrong: We delayed to book the tickets.
right: We delayed booking the tickets.
why: After delay, use the -ing form of the verb.
ex: Do not delay answering the email.
They delayed leaving until noon.

quiz.explain: Delay is followed by a verb with -ing.

point: interested (adj): wanting to know or do more
wrong: I am interested for English music.
right: I am interested in English music.
why: Use the preposition in after interested.
aha: Interested pairs with in, like 'in the box'.
ex: She is interested in art.
Are you interested in joining us?

quiz.explain: Use the preposition in after interested.

point: information (n): facts about something (uncountable)
wrong: Can you give me some informations about the course?
right: Can you give me some information about the course?
why: Information is uncountable, so it has no plural -s.
ex: I need more information.
The website has useful information.

quiz.explain: Information is uncountable, so it has no plural -s.

point: interview (n): a formal meeting where someone asks you questions
wrong: I make a job interview on Monday.
right: I have a job interview on Monday.
why: We have an interview. We do not make one.
aha: Think have an interview, like have a meeting.
ex: She has an interview at nine.
How was your interview?

quiz.q: I ___ a job interview on Monday.
quiz.explain: We have an interview. We do not make one.

point: increase (v): to become or make bigger
wrong: Prices increase up every year.
right: Prices increase every year.
why: Increase already means go up, so do not add up.
ex: The shop increased its prices.
The number of visitors increases in summer.

quiz.explain: Increase already means go up, so do not add up.

point: introduce (v): to tell people each other's names
wrong: Let me introduce about myself.
right: Let me introduce myself.
why: Introduce takes the person directly, so do not add about.
aha: Say introduce, then the person. No about.
ex: Let me introduce my sister.
She introduced me to her friends.

quiz.explain: Introduce takes the person directly, so do not add about.

point: involve (v): to include or take part
wrong: She involved in the project last year.
right: She was involved in the project last year.
why: For a person taking part, say be involved in.
ex: Many students are involved in the club.
I don't want to get involved in it.

quiz.q: He is ___ in a school project.
quiz.explain: For a person taking part, say be involved in.

point: impress (v): to make someone admire you
wrong: I was impressed about her speech.
right: I was impressed by her speech.
why: After impressed, use by or with, not about.
aha: Impressed pairs with by or with.
ex: Her English impressed the teacher.
I was impressed with the hotel.

quiz.explain: After impressed, use by or with, not about.

point: insist (v): to say firmly that something must happen
wrong: He insisted to pay for dinner.
right: He insisted on paying for dinner.
why: Insist is followed by on and an -ing form.
ex: She insists on walking to work.
They insisted on a refund.

quiz.explain: Insist is followed by on and an -ing form.

point: instead (adv): in place of something else
wrong: I took the bus instead the train.
right: I took the bus instead of the train.
why: Before a noun, use instead of. Instead alone has no noun after it.
ex: It was raining, so we stayed home instead.
Have tea instead of coffee.

quiz.explain: Before a noun, use instead of. Instead alone has no noun after it.

point: ill (adj): not well; sick
wrong: I can't come because I am illness.
right: I can't come because I am ill.
why: Ill is the adjective. Illness is the noun.
aha: After am, use the adjective ill.
ex: He was ill for a week.
She felt ill after lunch.

quiz.q: I can't go because I am ___.
quiz.explain: Ill is the adjective. Illness is the noun.

point: idea (n): a thought or plan
hook: Natives don't say 'a good idea go'
wrong: It is a good idea go by train.
right: It is a good idea to go by train.
why: After a good idea, use to plus the verb.
ex: That is a great idea.
I have no idea where he is.

quiz.explain: After a good idea, use to plus the verb.

point: imagine (v): to make a picture in your mind
wrong: I can't imagine to live without music.
right: I can't imagine living without music.
why: Imagine is followed by an -ing form, not to.
ex: Imagine living on the moon.
I imagined the beach all day.

quiz.explain: Imagine is followed by an -ing form, not to.

point: invest (v): to put money into something to make more
wrong: He invested all his money on a small farm.
right: He invested all his money in a small farm.
why: Use invest in something, not invest on.
aha: Invest IN, like put money in.
ex: She wants to invest in a new business.
They invested in solar power.

quiz.q: She wants to invest ___ a new business.
quiz.explain: Use invest in something, not invest on.

point: join (v): to become a member of or meet a group
wrong: I want to join to the English club.
right: I want to join the English club.
why: Join takes the group directly, with no to.
ex: Please join us for dinner.
He joined a football team.

quiz.explain: Join takes the group directly, with no to.

point: joke (n): something funny you say to make people laugh
wrong: Can you say a joke?
right: Can you tell a joke?
why: We tell a joke. We do not say one.
aha: Tell a story, tell a joke.
ex: He told a funny joke.
That joke made me laugh.

quiz.explain: We tell a joke. We do not say one.

point: keep (v): to stay in a state or continue
wrong: Let's keep contact after the course.
right: Let's keep in touch after the course.
why: The fixed phrase is keep in touch.
aha: Keep in touch, like a quick text.
ex: Keep the door closed.
We keep in touch by email.

quiz.explain: The fixed phrase is keep in touch.

point: knock (v): to hit a door to ask to come in
wrong: Please knock the door first.
right: Please knock on the door first.
why: Use knock on a door, with the preposition on.
aha: Knock ON wood, knock ON a door.
ex: Someone is knocking on the window.
Knock before you come in.

quiz.explain: Use knock on a door, with the preposition on.

point: know (v): to have information in your mind
wrong: I am knowing the answer now.
right: I know the answer now.
why: Know is a state verb, so we do not use -ing.
aha: State verbs like know stay simple.
ex: I know his name.
Do you know the way?

quiz.explain: Know is a state verb, so we do not use -ing.

point: knowledge (n): what you know; information in your mind
wrong: She has many knowledges about computers.
right: She has a lot of knowledge about computers.
why: Knowledge is uncountable, so it has no -s and no many.
aha: Knowledge is like water: no plural.
ex: He has good knowledge of history.
Reading gives you knowledge.

quiz.q: He has a lot of ___ about cars.
quiz.explain: Knowledge is uncountable, so it has no -s and no many.

point: knife (n): a tool with a blade for cutting
wrong: Please bring two knifes.
right: Please bring two knives.
why: The plural of knife is knives.
aha: Knife becomes knives, like wife and wives.
ex: Cut the bread with a knife.
The knives are in the drawer.

quiz.explain: The plural of knife is knives.

point: late (adv): after the expected time
wrong: I arrived lately at the station.
right: I arrived late at the station.
why: Late is also an adverb. Lately means recently.
aha: Late = not on time. Lately = recently.
ex: The train arrived late.
I went to bed late last night.

quiz.explain: Late is also an adverb. Lately means recently.

point: laugh (v): to make a happy sound at something funny
wrong: Don't laugh me.
right: Don't laugh at me.
why: Laugh needs at before the person or thing.
aha: Laugh AT someone, look AT someone.
ex: We laughed at the film.
The children laughed all day.

quiz.explain: Laugh needs at before the person or thing.

point: learn (v): to get knowledge or a skill
wrong: My father learned me to swim.
right: My father taught me to swim.
why: Learn is for the student. Teach is for the person giving lessons.
ex: I learn ten new words a day.
She learned to drive last year.

quiz.explain: Learn is for the student. Teach is for the person giving lessons.

point: leave (v): to go away from a place
wrong: I leave from home at seven.
right: I leave home at seven.
why: Leave takes a place directly, so do not add from.
ex: He left the office early.
We leave home at six.

quiz.explain: Leave takes a place directly, so do not add from.

point: lend (v): to give something for a short time
wrong: Can you borrow me your pen?
right: Can you lend me your pen?
why: Lend means you give it. Borrow means you take it.
aha: You lend to others, borrow from others.
ex: I can lend you my bike.
She lent me ten dollars.

quiz.explain: Lend means you give it. Borrow means you take it.

point: lot (n): a large amount or number
wrong: I have a lots of homework.
right: I have a lot of homework.
why: Use a lot of, with lot in the singular.
aha: A lot of, or lots of. Never a lots.
ex: We have a lot of time.
She eats a lot of fruit.

quiz.explain: Use a lot of, with lot in the singular.

point: luck (n): good things that happen by chance
wrong: Good luck for your exam!
right: Good luck with your exam!
why: Say good luck with something.
ex: Good luck with your new job!
He had bad luck yesterday.

quiz.explain: Say good luck with something.

point: last (adj): just before now
wrong: I visited Hue the last week.
right: I visited Hue last week.
why: Do not use the before last in phrases like last week.
aha: Last week, last month. No the.
ex: I saw her last month.
What did you do last night?

quiz.explain: Do not use the before last in phrases like last week.

point: like (v): to enjoy or find pleasant
wrong: I am like Vietnamese food.
right: I like Vietnamese food.
why: Like is already the main verb. Do not add am.
aha: I like. Not I am like.
ex: I like tea in the morning.
Do you like football?
memory: Like is the verb, no am

quiz.explain: Like is already the main verb. Do not add am.

point: live (v): to have your home in a place
wrong: My family lives at Hanoi.
right: My family lives in Hanoi.
why: Use in with cities and countries after live.
ex: They live in a small town.
Where do you live?

quiz.explain: Use in with cities and countries after live.

point: luggage (n): bags and cases you take on a trip
wrong: I have two luggages.
right: I have two pieces of luggage.
why: Luggage is uncountable. Use pieces of luggage to count it.
ex: Your luggage is heavy.
I lost my luggage at the airport.

quiz.explain: Luggage is uncountable. Use pieces of luggage to count it.

point: life (n): the time you are alive
wrong: Many lifes were saved.
right: Many lives were saved.
why: The plural of life is lives.
aha: Life becomes lives, like knife and knives.
ex: Life is hard but fun.
Doctors save lives every day.

quiz.explain: The plural of life is lives.

point: manage (v): to succeed in doing something difficult
wrong: I managed finding a cheap hotel.
right: I managed to find a cheap hotel.
why: Manage is followed by to plus a verb.
ex: She managed to open the door.
I managed to finish on time.

quiz.explain: Manage is followed by to plus a verb.

point: mention (v): to say something briefly
wrong: He mentioned about the problem.
right: He mentioned the problem.
why: Mention takes its object directly, so do not add about.
ex: She didn't mention the price.
Did he mention my name?

quiz.explain: Mention takes its object directly, so do not add about.

point: mind (v): to be annoyed or bothered by something
wrong: Do you mind to open the window?
right: Do you mind opening the window?
why: Mind is followed by an -ing form.
ex: Would you mind closing the door?
I don't mind waiting.

quiz.explain: Mind is followed by an -ing form.

point: money (n): coins and notes used to buy things
wrong: I don't have many money.
right: I don't have much money.
why: Money is uncountable, so use much, not many.
ex: She spends money on books.
I saved some money last year.

quiz.explain: Money is uncountable, so use much, not many.

point: most (adj): nearly all of a group
wrong: Most of people like music.
right: Most people like music.
why: Use most alone before a plain noun. Use most of before the or my.
aha: Most people, but most of the people.
ex: Most students here are young.
Most days I walk to school.

quiz.explain: Use most alone before a plain noun. Use most of before the or my.

point: mistake (n): something done wrongly
wrong: I did a mistake in the test.
right: I made a mistake in the test.
why: Mistake goes with make, not do.
aha: Make a mistake, make a plan.
ex: It was my mistake.
Everyone makes mistakes.

quiz.explain: Mistake goes with make, not do.

point: music (n): sounds made by instruments or voices
wrong: I like Korean musics.
right: I like Korean music.
why: Music is uncountable, so it has no plural.
aha: Music has no plural, like water.
ex: I listen to music every day.
She plays music in the shop.

quiz.explain: Music is uncountable, so it has no plural.

point: medicine (n): something you take to treat an illness
wrong: I ate some medicine for my cough.
right: I took some medicine for my cough.
why: We take medicine. We do not eat it.
ex: Take this medicine twice a day.
The medicine tastes bad.

quiz.q: You should ___ this medicine twice a day.
quiz.explain: We take medicine. We do not eat it.

point: maybe (adv): perhaps
hook: Natives don't say 'May be it will rain'
wrong: May be it will rain tomorrow.
right: Maybe it will rain tomorrow.
why: At the start of a sentence, write maybe as one word.
ex: Maybe we can meet on Friday.
Maybe he is at home.

quiz.explain: At the start of a sentence, write maybe as one word.

point: must (v): used for something very important or required
wrong: I must to finish this today.
right: I must finish this today.
why: After must, use the base verb without to.
aha: Must is a modal: no to.
ex: You must wear a seat belt.
I must go now.

quiz.explain: After must, use the base verb without to.

point: need (v): to want something because you have to have it
wrong: My car needs to wash.
right: My car needs washing.
why: When the thing receives the action, use needs plus -ing.
ex: The room needs cleaning.
Your hair needs cutting.

quiz.explain: When the thing receives the action, use needs plus -ing.

point: news (n): new information about events
wrong: The news are good today.
right: The news is good today.
why: News looks plural but is uncountable, so it takes is.
ex: The news is on at six.
I have some good news.

quiz.explain: News looks plural but is uncountable, so it takes is.

point: nature (n): plants, animals and the natural world
wrong: I love the nature.
right: I love nature.
why: Use nature without the when talking about the natural world in general.
ex: She loves walking in nature.
Nature is beautiful here.

quiz.explain: Use nature without the when talking about the natural world in general.

point: notice (v): to see or become aware of something
wrong: I didn't notice about the sign.
right: I didn't notice the sign.
why: Notice takes its object directly, so do not add about.
ex: Did you notice his new hair?
I noticed a strange sound.

quiz.explain: Notice takes its object directly, so do not add about.

point: next (adj): coming after this one
wrong: I will see you the next week.
right: I will see you next week.
why: Do not use the before next in phrases like next week.
aha: Next week, next year. No the.
ex: See you next Monday.
I travel next month.

quiz.explain: Do not use the before next in phrases like next week.

point: nowadays (adv): at the present time
wrong: In nowadays, many people use phones.
right: Nowadays, many people use phones.
why: Nowadays is an adverb, so do not put in before it.
ex: Nowadays, many people shop online.
Nowadays I walk to work.

quiz.explain: Nowadays is an adverb, so do not put in before it.

point: name (n): what someone or something is called
hook: Natives don't say 'My name is called'
wrong: My name is called Lan.
right: My name is Lan.
why: Say my name is Lan, or I am called Lan.
aha: My name is, or I am called.
ex: What is your name?
His name is Minh.

quiz.explain: Say my name is Lan, or I am called Lan.

point: nervous (adj): worried or a little afraid
wrong: I'm nervous with the exam.
right: I'm nervous about the exam.
why: After nervous, use about before the thing you worry about.
ex: She felt nervous before the test.
I'm nervous about my speech.

quiz.explain: After nervous, use about before the thing you worry about.

point: pay (v): give money; pay attention
wrong: You should pay more attention on your spelling.
right: You should pay more attention to your spelling.
why: We pay attention TO something, not ON it.
aha: Attention goes TO: pay attention to.
ex: Please pay attention to the teacher.
I paid for the tickets.

quiz.explain: Pay attention to something.

point: prefer (v): like one thing more
hook: Natives don't say 'prefer tea than coffee'
wrong: I prefer tea than coffee.
right: I prefer tea to coffee.
why: Use prefer A to B for two things. Do not use than.
aha: Prefer pairs with TO, not THAN.
ex: I prefer trains to buses.
She prefers walking to driving.

quiz.explain: Prefer A to B.

point: provide (v): give what someone needs
wrong: The school provides us books.
right: The school provides us with books.
why: Provide someone WITH something, or provide something for someone.
ex: The hotel provides free breakfast.
They provided us with maps.

quiz.explain: Provide someone with something.

point: prevent (v): stop something happening
hook: Natives don't say 'prevent me to go'
wrong: The rain prevented us to go out.
right: The rain prevented us from going out.
why: After prevent plus a person, use from and an -ing word.
ex: Good locks prevent theft.
Nothing can prevent him from winning.

quiz.explain: Prevent someone from doing something.

point: participate (v): take part in
wrong: Many students participated the contest.
right: Many students participated in the contest.
why: Participate needs the word in before the activity.
ex: Everyone can participate in the game.
I participated in a school trip.

quiz.explain: Participate needs in.

point: reply (v): answer someone
wrong: Please reply me soon.
right: Please reply to me soon.
why: Reply needs to before the person or message.
ex: I replied to her email.
He did not reply to my message.

quiz.explain: Reply needs to.

point: refuse (v): say no
wrong: He refused going to the meeting.
right: He refused to go to the meeting.
why: Refuse is followed by to and the base verb.
aha: Refuse TO do, not refuse doing.
ex: She refused to wait.
They refused my offer.

quiz.explain: Refuse is followed by to plus verb.

point: spend (v): use time or money
hook: Natives don't say 'spend two hours to do'
wrong: I spend two hours to do my homework.
right: I spend two hours doing my homework.
why: After spend time, use an -ing verb, not to.
ex: We spent the weekend cleaning.
She spends a lot of money on clothes.

quiz.explain: Spend time plus -ing.

point: search (v): look carefully for
wrong: I am searching a new job.
right: I am searching for a new job.
why: Search for the thing you want to find.
ex: The police searched the house.
I searched for my keys.

quiz.explain: Search for what you want.

point: succeed (v): reach a goal
wrong: She succeeded to pass the exam.
right: She succeeded in passing the exam.
why: Succeed is followed by in and an -ing verb.
ex: He succeeded in finding a job.
We succeeded in the end.

quiz.explain: Succeed in doing.

point: wait (v): stay until something comes
wrong: I am waiting you at the gate.
right: I am waiting for you at the gate.
why: Wait needs for before the person or thing.
ex: Wait for me here.
We waited for the bus.

quiz.explain: Wait needs for.

point: return (v): go or come back
wrong: He returned back to Hanoi yesterday.
right: He returned to Hanoi yesterday.
why: Return already means come back. Do not add back.
aha: Return = go back, so no back.
ex: She returned the book.
They return home on Friday.

quiz.explain: Return already means back.

point: weather (n): rain, sun, wind
wrong: We had a lovely weathers on holiday.
right: We had lovely weather on holiday.
why: Weather is uncountable. It has no plural and no a.
ex: The weather is hot today.
What is the weather like?

quiz.explain: Weather is uncountable.

point: scenery (n): beautiful views of nature
wrong: The sceneries in Sapa are beautiful.
right: The scenery in Sapa is beautiful.
why: Scenery is uncountable, so it has no plural.
aha: Scenery is one thing: no s.
ex: We enjoyed the mountain scenery.
The scenery was amazing.

quiz.explain: Scenery has no plural.

point: permission (n): OK from someone
wrong: I need a permission to leave early.
right: I need permission to leave early.
why: Permission is uncountable. Do not use a before it.
aha: Ask for permission, never a permission.
ex: You need permission to park here.
She gave me permission to go.

quiz.explain: Permission is uncountable.

point: traffic (n): cars on the road
wrong: There are many traffics in the city.
right: There is a lot of traffic in the city.
why: Traffic is uncountable, so use a lot of, not many.
ex: The traffic was bad this morning.
Heavy traffic made me late.
memory: Traffic: a lot of, not many

quiz.q: There is a lot of ___ at 5 pm.
quiz.explain: Traffic is uncountable.

point: work (n): jobs and tasks
hook: Natives don't say 'a lot of works'
wrong: I have a lot of works to do today.
right: I have a lot of work to do today.
why: Work meaning a job or tasks is uncountable. No s.
aha: Work, no s: a lot of work.
ex: I have too much work today.
Her work is hard but fun.

quiz.explain: Work is uncountable.

point: offer (v): say you will give or do
wrong: He offered helping me with the bags.
right: He offered to help me with the bags.
why: Offer is followed by to and the base verb.
ex: She offered to drive us home.
They offered me a job.

quiz.explain: Offer is followed by to plus verb.

point: oppose (v): be against
wrong: Many people oppose against the new road.
right: Many people oppose the new road.
why: Oppose already means be against. Do not add against.
aha: Oppose = be against, so no against.
ex: Some neighbours oppose the plan.
I oppose this idea.

quiz.explain: Oppose takes no against.

point: rather (adv): more willingly
hook: Natives don't say 'would rather to stay'
wrong: I would rather to stay at home tonight.
right: I would rather stay at home tonight.
why: After would rather, use the base verb without to.
ex: I would rather walk than take a bus.
She would rather have tea.

quiz.explain: No to after would rather.

point: quiet (adj): with little noise
wrong: Please be quite. The baby is sleeping.
right: Please be quiet. The baby is sleeping.
why: Quiet means not noisy. Quite means fairly or very.
ex: The street is quiet at night.
He is a quiet boy.

quiz.explain: Quiet means not noisy.

point: satisfied (adj): happy with what you got
wrong: I am not satisfied of the service.
right: I am not satisfied with the service.
why: Be satisfied WITH something. Of is not used.
ex: She is satisfied with her score.
Are you satisfied with the room?

quiz.q: He is satisfied ___ his new phone.
quiz.explain: Satisfied with something.

point: surprised (adj): feeling that something is unexpected
wrong: I was surprised for his answer.
right: I was surprised at his answer.
why: Use surprised at or surprised by before the cause.
ex: We were surprised at the news.
She was surprised by the gift.

quiz.explain: Surprised at or by.

point: sensible (adj): showing good sense
wrong: She cries at sad films. She is very sensible.
right: She cries at sad films. She is very sensitive.
why: Sensible means showing good sense. Sensitive means easily moved or hurt.
ex: That is a sensible idea.
Wear sensible shoes for the walk.

quiz.q: It is ___ to take an umbrella.
quiz.explain: Sensible means showing good sense.

point: sound (v): seem when heard
wrong: That sounds like good.
right: That sounds good.
why: After sound, use an adjective directly. Use like before a noun.
aha: Sounds plus adjective; sounds like plus noun.
ex: Your plan sounds great.
That sounds like fun.

quiz.explain: Use an adjective directly after sound.

point: waste (v): use badly
hook: Natives don't say 'waste time to wait'
wrong: I wasted a lot of time to wait for the bus.
right: I wasted a lot of time waiting for the bus.
why: After waste time, use an -ing verb, not to.
ex: Don't waste money on cheap things.
He wastes hours playing games.

quiz.explain: Waste time plus -ing.

point: tired (adj): bored or needing rest
wrong: I am tired for waiting.
right: I am tired of waiting.
why: Tired of means bored or annoyed. Use of before the cause.
ex: I'm tired of this rain.
She is tired after work.

quiz.explain: Tired of the cause.

point: wear (v): have clothes on
wrong: She is wearing a glasses.
right: She is wearing glasses.
why: Glasses is always plural, so do not use a before it.
aha: Glasses, jeans, shorts: plural, no a.
ex: He wears a blue hat.
I wear glasses to read.

quiz.explain: Glasses is plural.

point: stay (v): live in a place for a short time
hook: Natives don't say 'stay in Hanoi, born'
wrong: I have stayed in Hanoi since I was born.
right: I have lived in Hanoi since I was born.
why: Stay means a short time. Use live for your home.
ex: We stayed at a small hotel.
Please stay here.

quiz.q: I ___ in Hue. I was born here.
quiz.explain: Use live for your home.

point: pair (n): two things together
wrong: I bought a new jeans yesterday.
right: I bought a new pair of jeans yesterday.
why: Jeans has two legs, so use a pair of.
aha: Jeans, shoes, glasses: a pair of.
ex: I need a pair of socks.
She lost a pair of gloves.

quiz.explain: Use a pair of with jeans.

point: ought (v): should
wrong: You ought go to the doctor.
right: You ought to go to the doctor.
why: Ought is always followed by to and the base verb.
ex: We ought to leave now.
You ought to rest.

quiz.explain: Ought needs to.

point: tall (adj): high, for people
wrong: My brother is a high man.
right: My brother is a tall man.
why: Use tall for people. Use high for things like walls.
aha: Tall for people, high for places.
ex: She is tall for her age.
A tall tree stood there.

quiz.explain: Use tall for people.

point: taste (v): have a flavour
wrong: The soup tastes well.
right: The soup tastes good.
why: After taste, use an adjective, not an adverb.
ex: This tea tastes sweet.
It tastes like chicken.

quiz.explain: Use an adjective after taste.

point: smell (v): have a smell
wrong: The kitchen smells deliciously.
right: The kitchen smells delicious.
why: After smell, use an adjective, not an adverb.
ex: The flowers smell lovely.
Something smells bad.

quiz.explain: Use an adjective after smell.

point: photo (n): picture from a camera
wrong: Let me make a photo of you.
right: Let me take a photo of you.
why: We take a photo. We do not make one.
aha: Take a photo, take a picture.
ex: She took a photo of the beach.
I like this photo.

quiz.q: Can you ___ a photo of us?
quiz.explain: We take photos.

point: ready (adj): prepared
hook: Natives don't say 'ready to the exam'
wrong: I'm ready to the exam.
right: I'm ready for the exam.
why: Use ready for before a noun. Use ready to before a verb.
aha: Ready FOR noun, ready TO verb.
ex: Are you ready for dinner?
I am ready to go.

quiz.explain: Ready for a noun.

point: scared (adj): afraid
wrong: I am scared from dogs.
right: I am scared of dogs.
why: Use scared of before the thing you fear.
ex: She is scared of spiders.
Don't be scared.

quiz.explain: Scared of something.

point: proud (adj): happy about success
wrong: My parents are proud about me.
right: My parents are proud of me.
why: Be proud of someone or something.
ex: I am proud of my team.
She felt proud.

quiz.explain: Proud of someone.

point: pleased (adj): happy
wrong: I am pleased meeting you.
right: I am pleased to meet you.
why: After pleased, use to and the base verb.
ex: I'm pleased to see you.
He was pleased with the result.

quiz.explain: Pleased to meet you.

point: worth (adj): good enough for the effort
wrong: This museum is worth to visit.
right: This museum is worth visiting.
why: After worth, use an -ing verb, not to.
ex: The film is worth seeing.
It is worth the money.

quiz.explain: Worth takes -ing.

point: tend (v): usually do
wrong: Young people tend using phones a lot.
right: Young people tend to use phones a lot.
why: Tend is followed by to and the base verb.
ex: I tend to wake up early.
Prices tend to rise in summer.

quiz.explain: Tend is followed by to.

point: pretend (v): act as if true
wrong: He pretended being sick.
right: He pretended to be sick.
why: Pretend is followed by to and the base verb.
ex: The children pretend to be pilots.
She pretended not to see me.

quiz.explain: Pretend is followed by to.

point: price (n): money to pay
wrong: The price of this phone is very cheap.
right: The price of this phone is very low.
why: A price is high or low. Things are cheap.
aha: Price: high or low; goods: cheap.
ex: The price of rice went up.
I checked the price.

quiz.explain: A price is low or high.

point: used (adj): familiar with
hook: Natives don't say 'used to get up'
wrong: I am used to get up early.
right: I am used to getting up early.
why: Be used to is followed by an -ing verb or a noun.
ex: She is used to the cold.
I'm used to walking.

quiz.explain: Be used to takes -ing.

point: vote (v): choose in an election
wrong: I will vote to Anna.
right: I will vote for Anna.
why: Vote for the person or idea you choose.
ex: Did you vote in the election?
Many people voted for her.

quiz.explain: Vote for someone.

point: stop (v): not do any more
wrong: He stopped to smoke last year.
right: He stopped smoking last year.
why: Stop doing means quit. Stop to do means stop in order to do.
ex: We stopped to buy water.
Please stop talking.

quiz.explain: Stop doing means quit.

point: reach (v): arrive at
wrong: We reached to the hotel at night.
right: We reached the hotel at night.
why: Reach is followed directly by a place. No to.
ex: We reached the top.
When do we reach Hue?

quiz.q: The bus will ___ Hue at six.
quiz.explain: Reach takes no to.

point: visit (v): go to see
wrong: I will visit to my grandmother.
right: I will visit my grandmother.
why: Visit is followed directly by a person or place. No to.
ex: We visited the museum.
She visits her aunt on Sundays.

quiz.explain: Visit takes no to.

point: survive (v): stay alive after
wrong: He survived from the accident.
right: He survived the accident.
why: Survive is followed directly by the event. No from.
ex: Few plants survive the cold.
She survived the crash.

quiz.explain: Survive takes no from.

point: walk (v): go on foot
wrong: I walk to home every day.
right: I walk home every day.
why: Home has no to after walk, go or come.
aha: Walk home, go home: no to.
ex: We walked home together.
She walks to school.

quiz.explain: No to before home.
